description: Nine barriers to sport participation, matched solutions, and how clubs remove them.
content_html:
Why Don’t People Participate?

Even when sport is on offer, many people never take part — or stop taking part. A barrier to participation is anything that gets in the way of someone being active. Understanding barriers is essential for sports clubs, leisure centres and national organisations because solving the wrong problem wastes resources. Identifying the right barrier for the right user group is the first step to removing it.

Key Fact

The nine barriers to participation are: employment and unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, media coverage (gender and ethnicity), and personal factors such as low self-esteem or perceived risk.

Employment and Unemployment

People in full-time employment often struggle to find time for sport around working hours, especially shift workers whose patterns change week to week. Unemployed people face the opposite problem — time may be available but money is scarce. For both groups, sport that is free or very low-cost and offered at flexible times is most likely to work. A solution for full-time workers might be a leisure centre that opens at 6 am and offers 45-minute express sessions.

Family Commitments

Parenting young children, caring for elderly relatives, or running a household all compete with time for sport. Single parents and carers are particularly affected because they often have no one to share these responsibilities with. Solutions include ‘buggy fitness’ classes where children attend alongside parents, family membership schemes, and on-site crèche provision at leisure centres. Creche availability is frequently cited by mothers as the single most important factor in their ability to exercise.

Disposable income is the money left over after essential bills are paid. Sport has many hidden costs beyond a club membership fee: kit, footwear, travel, match fees, specialist coaching and competition entry all add up. For economically disadvantaged families, these costs can put participation out of reach entirely. Solutions include concessionary pricing (discounted entry for those on benefits or low incomes), kit-swap schemes run by local authorities, and Sport England ‘Active Communities’ grants that fund free holiday sport programmes.

Lack of Transport

Sport facilities are not evenly distributed across the country. In rural areas, there may be no swimming pool, athletics track or sports hall within reasonable distance, and public transport links may be poor or non-existent. Even in cities, night-time training sessions can end after the last bus. Solutions include minibus schemes organised by clubs, locating new facilities on existing public transport corridors, and encouraging car-sharing among club members.

Lack of Role Models

Seeing someone who looks like you succeeding in a sport increases belief that participation is possible. The absence of visible role models from ethnic minority backgrounds, disability sport, or specific genders at elite level can make sport feel ‘not for people like me.’ Solutions include targeted media campaigns, athlete ambassador programmes, and ensuring representative coaches at grassroots level. The visibility of British wheelchair tennis players and blind footballers at Paris 2024 inspired thousands of young disabled people to enquire about their local clubs.

Some user groups — such as carers, retired people or people with certain disabilities — simply find that no suitable programme exists near them. A leisure centre that offers only five-a-side football and high-intensity circuits has not provided for these groups at all. Solution: sports clubs can create targeted programmes (walking netball, sitting volleyball, adapted badminton) specifically for underrepresented groups.

Even where provision exists, people may not know about it. Lack of awareness is particularly common among newer immigrant communities who are unfamiliar with local sport structures, and among older adults who may not use social media. Solutions include targeted promotion through community centres, GP referral schemes, leafleting in non-English languages, and word-of-mouth outreach through trusted community leaders.

Media Coverage: Gender and Ethnicity

The sports that receive the most media coverage attract the most participants. Women’s sport and disability sport have historically received far less broadcast time and newspaper coverage than men’s sport. This creates a cycle: less coverage means fewer visible role models, which means fewer women and disabled people try those sports, which means fewer compelling stories for broadcasters to cover. The growth in women’s football audiences — the Women’s Super League regularly drew over one million TV viewers per match in 2024-25 — shows how media investment can shift participation patterns.

Key Fact

Examiners reward barrier–solution pairings. The question will say ‘identify one barrier for [user group] and suggest one solution.’ A barrier without a matched solution, or a solution without a linked barrier, typically scores only half the available marks.

Solutions: Facility Access and Adapted Provision

Physical adapted provision is essential for people with disabilities. This includes wheelchair-accessible changing rooms and pool hoists for swimmers, hearing loops at reception and in fitness studios, braille signage for visually impaired users, and coaching qualifications that cover disability sport. A sports facility that lacks a pool hoist has effectively excluded all wheelchair users from aquatic activity, regardless of how welcoming the staff are.

Solutions: Pricing, Promotion and Taster Sessions

Concessionary pricing reduces cost barriers: councils and leisure trusts typically offer discounts to people on Universal Credit, Job Seekers’ Allowance, or disability benefits. Taster sessions — free, no-kit-required introductory classes — lower the psychological barrier of trying something unfamiliar. Targeted promotion means advertising where the target group already is: leaflets at food banks for economically disadvantaged families, posters in GP waiting rooms for retired people, and social media campaigns in minority languages for ethnic minority communities.

A very common error is to list several barriers and then separately list several solutions, without showing which solution addresses which barrier. The question typically asks you to identify a barrier and then suggest how to overcome it for a specific user group. The mark is awarded for the linkage — barrier X causes problem Y for group Z; solution A removes barrier X by doing B. Always write your answer as a chain, not two separate lists.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘suggest a solution to a barrier’, make sure your solution directly addresses the barrier you named — not just any barrier. For example, if the barrier is ‘lack of transport’, a relevant solution is ‘a club minibus scheme’; saying ‘build more facilities’ would not directly remove the transport barrier and will not score. For ‘discuss’ questions, consider two or more user groups or two or more barriers — examiners reward answers that consider more than one viewpoint.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are nine barriers: employment/unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, and media coverage relating to gender and ethnicity.
  • Solutions must be matched to the specific barrier and user group — the linkage is what earns exam marks, not separate lists.
  • Adapted provision (hoists, hearing loops, braille signage), concessionary pricing, taster sessions and targeted promotion are the main solution categories to learn.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a barrier to participation in sport?
A) High media coverage of women's sport
B) Lack of disposable income
C) Availability of concessionary pricing
D) Strong role models
practice_questions.marks: B) Lack of disposable income [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two solutions a sports club could use to increase participation among people with disabilities.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: pool hoists / wheelchair-accessible changing rooms / hearing loops / braille signage / adapted equipment / disability-specific coaching / adapted programmes such as sitting volleyball / wheelchair basketball. Accept any two genuinely different answers. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lack of role models acts as a barrier to participation for ethnic minorities.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic point (e.g. 'if there are no role models from that background, people may feel the sport is not for them'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'if ethnic minority young people do not see athletes from their background succeeding in a sport, they may not believe they could succeed themselves, which reduces motivation to try'). 3 marks for a fuller explanation or a second distinct reason applied to ethnic minorities (e.g. add 'in addition, clubs may seem culturally unfamiliar if all the coaches and committee members are from a different background, which reinforces the sense of not belonging'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the barrier of 'lack of transport' and explain one solution a sports club could offer to overcome this barrier for unemployed people.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): lack of transport means that people cannot get to sports facilities because they live far away, have no car, or public transport is limited or unavailable at the times sessions are held (2 marks for clear description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Solution with example (up to 2 marks): the club could organise a minibus to collect members from a central meeting point, funded by a community grant, which removes the transport cost and logistics barrier for unemployed people who may not be able to afford a car or taxi (2 marks for a clear, applied solution; 1 mark for a vague suggestion). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Ferndale Leisure Trust has identified that participation among single parents in their local area is very low. They have a limited budget.

Discuss the barriers single parents face when trying to participate in sport and how the leisure trust could overcome them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion that names at least two specific barriers (e.g. family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of suitable provision) and matches each to a realistic solution within a limited budget (e.g. crèche provision on-site, concessionary pricing, taster sessions at no cost, family swim sessions). Both barriers and solutions are clearly linked and the answer considers more than one perspective or challenge.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two barriers identified with some linked solutions, though development may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One barrier and one solution, or two barriers with no solutions.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Northgate Athletics Club has applied for a grant to improve participation among economically disadvantaged young people aged 11–16 in their town. The club is considering offering free taster sessions, subsidised kit loans, and a minibus from the town centre.

Evaluate how effective these three strategies are likely to be at removing the barriers faced by economically disadvantaged teenagers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that assesses all three strategies, explaining the specific barrier each targets (cost of trying, cost of kit, transport) and weighing effectiveness. The best answers argue that taster sessions remove the awareness and psychological barrier but not the ongoing cost barrier; subsidised kit loans address one major cost but not ongoing club fees; the minibus removes transport but only for those who know about the club and want to attend. A substantiated judgement is reached on which combination is most effective or what additional strategy would be needed.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more strategies evaluated with clear reasoning and some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Strategies described but evaluation is one-sided or judgement is missing.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about barriers or solutions with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is meant by 'disposable income' in the context of barriers to sport?
options: The money left over after essential bills are paid
Income earned through part-time sports work

knowledge_checks.q: A sports facility installs a pool hoist and a hearing loop. Which user group is most directly helped by these adaptations?
A leisure centre offering discounted entry fees to people on Universal Credit is using _____ pricing to overcome the barrier of lack of disposable income.
The absence of athletes from a particular background who have succeeded in a sport is called a lack of _____.
Match each barrier to the solution most likely to directly address it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a barrier to participation in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: A factor that prevents or reduces a person's ability or willingness to take part in sport.

flashcard_questions.q: How many barriers to participation are listed in the specification?

flashcard_questions.a: Money left after essential living costs such as housing and food are paid.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the barrier where no suitable sport programme exists near a user group.
A pool hoist at a leisure centre directly removes which barrier for people with disabilities?
flashcard_questions.a: Lack of adapted provision / restricted access to facilities.

flashcard_questions.q: What pricing strategy gives discounted entry to people on low incomes or benefits?
Why is a free introductory class called a taster session useful for overcoming barriers?
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces the psychological barrier of trying something unfamiliar at no cost.

flashcard_questions.q: Which barrier describes not knowing that a sport programme exists nearby?
What solution addresses the barrier of lack of transport in a rural area?
flashcard_questions.a: A club minibus scheme collecting members from a central point.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must an exam answer link a barrier to its matching solution?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the mark is awarded for the pairing, not for listing barriers and solutions separately.

flashcard_questions.q: What facility adaptation helps visually impaired users navigate a sports centre?
Which barrier is created when women's and disability sport receive very little broadcast coverage?
flashcard_questions.a: Media coverage — lack of visibility reduces role models and awareness for those groups.

glossary_terms.definition: A factor that prevents or reduces an individual's ability or willingness to participate in sport and physical activity.
People who do not have paid work and therefore have limited household income, which can restrict their access to sport.
The money a person has left over after paying for essential living costs such as housing, food and bills.
Changes made to a sports facility or programme to make it usable by people with a disability or specific need.

items.description: Real example of a sport programme designed to remove physical and social barriers for older adults — shows how adapted provision works in practice.

items.title: Cool Runnings (1993)
items.description: The Jamaican bobsled team overcomes financial, cultural and institutional barriers to reach the Winter Olympics — an entertaining lens on what it costs to participate against the odds.

items.description: Official Sport England pages on tackling inequality in sport: data on which groups participate least and what funded programmes are trying to fix it.

items.description: Practical guidance for sports clubs on removing barriers for disabled people: adapted provision, facility access and disability-inclusive coaching.

items.title: Influences on Participation — GCSE PE Revision (Revision App)
items.description: Short revision video covering the key factors that influence participation, useful for checking you can name and explain each barrier.

items.title: Sport England — Active Communities
items.description: Detail on the lottery-funded Active Communities programme, which provides free and low-cost sport in areas of high deprivation to tackle the disposable income barrier.

items.title: Women in Sport — Barriers to Female Participation
items.description: Research into the specific barriers women and girls face, including media coverage, role models and social acceptability — supports answers on the gender user group.
